Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I remember the event I feel intense shame
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

I can't stop bad things from happening to me
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The threat items are centered on interpersonal assault/paranoia from strangers and home-intrusion checking, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness. A clinician would expect threat to focus more on medical crises, loss, or signs of the child's deterioration rather than strangers harming the patient.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: Pain-on-recall implies a trauma involving direct bodily injury to the patient in specific body parts. That is difficult to fit with the indexed trauma being the child's illness, unless there was a separate bodily trauma not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is more typical of sexual assault or severe interpersonal violation and is not well supported by the rest of the profile or the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, pervasive threat specifically from strangers in ordinary situations is hard to reconcile unless there is another interpersonal or assault-related trauma. The other items center on fear, shame, silence, and baby-related cues rather than stranger danger, so this threat item is clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Re-experiencing physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is difficult to fit with the indexed trauma of a child's illness, because the trauma is primarily about the child's medical crisis rather than bodily injury to the patient. Without any other bodily injury cues elsewhere in the profile, this memory item is implausible.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling dirty or contaminated because of what happened is more characteristic of sexual trauma, assault, or severe moral injury involving bodily violation. It does not fit well with the rest of the profile for a parent's trauma about a child's illness, where guilt, responsibility, helplessness, or fear would be more coherent.

For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, 'Babies' as a trigger is hard to reconcile unless the child was specifically an infant; it is not impossible, but without any matching illness/hospital/medical cues elsewhere in the profile it stands out as a poor fit with the trauma context.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' suggests fear of intrusion or assault, but the rest of the profile centers on illness-related guilt, danger, and affective re-experiencing rather than a threat of external attack. This threat item is not well supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisal content and is clinically hard to integrate with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile unless there is some morally injurious action in the history. The rest of the profile points to fear, helplessness, and failure-to-protect themes rather than a clear values-violation theme, so this appraisal stands out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected
issues.explanation: 'Being criticised or corrected' is not impossible, but it is weakly connected to the rest of this profile. The other triggers and downstream items center on hospital-associated cues, silence, danger, shame, and failure to protect during the child's illness. Criticism/correction suggests an interpersonal evaluative pathway that is not otherwise represented in memory, threat, or appraisals, making it the least coherent trigger in this formulation.

Alcohol smell is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness unless there is additional context linking alcohol specifically to the illness setting or event. Hospital/antiseptic smell is coherent, but alcohol smell suggests a different trauma context and stands out as clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the accompanying appraisals. The selected appraisals center on danger, helplessness, and failure to protect, which fit guilt/self-blame more clearly than shame. As phrased, shame is somewhat mismatched with the rest of the node pattern.

For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, hospital/antiseptic smells and silence are plausible triggers, but a burnt smell implies a fire/burning context that is not represented anywhere else in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals. This looks trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I should have protected others and I failed' can fit caregiver trauma, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the demographic/trauma context of a child's serious illness, where direct preventability is often limited. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes global danger and helplessness rather than responsibility for causing/preventing harm, this item is the least coherent and may overstate a preventable-threat formulation not otherwise supported.

vignette:
Linh Tran is a 74-year-old Vietnamese American software engineer who came to treatment after years of living as if catastrophe might arrive the moment things went quiet. She is married and still works, mostly from home now, on a long-term contract role that lets her keep a structured routine. The event she returns to again and again is the period when her child became critically ill and was rushed to the hospital with a life-threatening condition. She describes that time less as a sequence than as a suspended state of dread: the drive to the emergency department with the sound of cars rushing past, the sharp antiseptic smell in the hallways, the abrupt silences between alarms and footsteps outside the room. What stays with her most is how those silences felt. When the corridor suddenly went still, she would stop breathing for a second, convinced that something terrible had already happened and no one had told her yet.

During the hospitalization, Linh spent long stretches in the child’s room trying to read staff faces, listening for movement, listening for any change. She remembers herself waiting for information and feeling she had no power to affect any of it. She has come to believe that those hours showed her something fundamental about life: that the world is dangerous, that disaster can appear without warning, and that when it does she cannot stop it. Alongside that helplessness is a painful self-accusation that has never fully softened. She is certain there was some way she acted wrong, some decision she should have made sooner or differently, and that this failure belongs to her. When she speaks about that period, shame rises quickly and seems to catch her off guard even after all these years.

In the months after her child survived, other people expected relief to settle in. Instead, Linh found that ordinary moments could turn charged without warning. The antiseptic smell of a clinic, a medical office, even certain cleaning products could make her chest tighten before she had time to think. The sound of cars outside, especially when she was being driven somewhere or hearing tires pass steadily on the street, pulled her back toward the trip to the hospital. Most unsettling of all was silence. If the house suddenly became completely still, if the refrigerator stopped humming, if conversation dropped away, she would feel a jolt of certainty that something dangerous was about to happen. She did not always picture the hospital clearly. Often there was no image at all, just the full force of terror in her body, as if the event were happening in the present.

Remembering the illness directly is also difficult. When she does recall it, she says the terror is not softened by time; it comes back with the same intensity she felt then. Just as often, shame arrives with it. She can be sitting at her desk reviewing code, paused between tasks in the unusual hush of her home office, and suddenly feel that familiar emotional flood with no clear mental picture attached. At work this has made her wary of quiet stretches. She keeps background audio on more than she used to and remains watchful for disruptions around her. Even during routine programming tasks, part of her attention is scanning—listening, monitoring, staying on guard. She describes this not as a choice but as something she feels she must do.

Sleep has become another arena where she feels she cannot let go. At night, when the house settles and the silence deepens, she has difficulty falling asleep because she feels she needs to stay alert. If she lets herself drift off too fully, it seems to her that she will miss the first sign of danger. Her husband has noticed that she startles at small sounds and that she often lies awake listening. Over time this constant alertness has narrowed their evenings. She is less able to relax with him in quiet companionship, because quiet itself no longer feels neutral.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was not a new trauma but the recognition that her life had become organized around anticipating harm. A recent moment in her home office—hearing traffic outside, then sudden total silence after a sound cut off—brought such a wave of terror and shame that she had to stop working. She found herself thinking, again, that the world is dangerous and that she will never be able to prevent the next terrible thing. She is seeking help now because she is exhausted by living so watchfully, but what frightens her most is the possibility that lowering her guard, even a little, would mean allowing disaster to happen again.
